podcast.title: Global Album Sales (Late 2002)
podcast.body: By late 2002, Sum 41 had not only sold many records in Canada but also millions around the world. "Some 41, not only sold a ton of records in Canada, but they also sold millions around the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 500th Show!

podcast.title: Derek Whibley's Health Catastrophe (May 2014)
podcast.body: In May 2014, Derek Whibley was hospitalized for approximately a month with "Leverie Kidney failure" (likely liver and kidney failure), followed by two to three months of outpatient care, largely supported by his mother, a nurse. During this time, he required hospital check-ups every other day. The illness caused severe physical and cognitive impairments, including muscle atrophy that prevented him from walking, and an inability to play guitar, make chords, form complete sentences, remember, or spell. He described it as "starting from zero for everything." "I was in hospital for about a month and then I was released but I was still like an outpatient. So luckily my mom's a nurse so she was with me the whole time for about another two or three months after that because I still needed to be in some kind of care."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Derek Whibley's Recovery & Return to Music (2014)
podcast.body: After his severe health crisis in May 2014, Derek Whibley embarked on a rigorous recovery, including daily physical therapy to regain his ability to walk and play guitar. By November 2014, he began writing music again and felt physically better. To reintegrate into the music world, he started attending concerts, including shows by Aerosmith and Fleetwood Mac, as he was unable to perform himself at the time. "I would say by November of 2014, I was starting to write music again and felt like I could kind of walk around, okay, and it was getting better."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: "Don't Call It A Some Back Tour"
podcast.body: The tour accompanying the "13 Voices" album was deliberately named "Don't Call It A Some Back Tour," humorously addressing the media's branding of the album as a comeback after a five-year gap and lineup changes. "So no wonder the subsequent tour was called Don't Call It A Some Back Tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: "Still Waiting" and Italian Recording Similarity
podcast.body: The Sum 41 hit "Still Waiting" was found by internet users to bear a strong resemblance to an Italian recording from the mid to late 1990s. Despite the striking likeness, this was categorized as an "unfortunate sonic coincidence" because pop songs often have simple structures, and the melody (based on two alternating notes punctuated by three or four more) could easily be independently discovered by different composers. "Sounds very, very similar, doesn't it? ... I'd simply chalk this up to unfortunate sonic coincidences and we're only aware of it because of the power and the reach of the internet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sonic Coincidences in Alt-Rock Part 1

podcast.title: Adapting to Music Industry Changes
podcast.body: Derek Whibley acknowledges the drastic changes in the music industry from CD sales to streaming but admits he doesn't fully understand the business models. He instead gauges the band's success by the increasing size of their live audiences, seeing bigger crowds every year and with every album. "I don't know if we're doing good. Well, or, you know, we just go out when we tour and we see people at the shows. And we know our shows are getting bigger everywhere we go."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Album Named After Rescuer
podcast.body: During the three days Sum 41 was trapped in a Congolese civil war zone, a UN official named Chuck bravely moved the band and 40 other people to safety within the hotel. Derek Whibley promised Chuck that if he got them out, they would name their next album after him. Chuck subsequently organized armored tanks to evacuate them. "Chuck, if you get us out of this, we're going to name this record after you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Artistic Philosophy of Constant Building
podcast.body: Derek Whibley believes that for a band like Sum 41, there's a constant need to build and prove themselves with each new record. He feels that every album is "like your first record" and that they should always be pushing their sound and capabilities further. "I feel like a record is always kind of like your first record. You've always got something to prove."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Back Injury Re-aggravated in Japan
podcast.body: Derek Whibley's chronic back injury flared up again after he was attacked by two or three guys from behind in a small bar in Japan, forcing the cancellation of the remaining tour dates. He returned home, but continued to cope with the pain through drinking instead of proper care, leading to ongoing chronic issues. "I was just... it was a friend of ours has this bar we've been going to for, you know, since we've been going to Japan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Band Formation & Early Success
podcast.body: Sum 41 formed during a summer vacation in the 1990s, with their initial period from 1996 through 2005 characterized by intense activity and rapid success, ultimately selling over 10 million records. "The band burned very hot and very bright from 1996 through to 2005."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Bidding War for Record Deal
podcast.body: After Michael McCarty at EMI Publishing signed Derek Whibley to a publishing deal at age 17 and began sending out Sum 41's demos, interest from record companies grew into a bidding war. Despite mixed initial reactions, the band eventually signed a worldwide deal with Island Def Jam, while Aquarius Records (the first label to show interest) retained the Canadian rights. "it turned into a bidding war for some reason. Like everything just sort of changed from what it was."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Canadian Origin
podcast.body: Sum 41 originated from Canada, where they achieved multi-platinum success and widespread recognition. "They broke out of Canada with a multi-platinum album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Pop Punk: Part 2

podcast.title: Career Launch and Production by Greg Nori
podcast.body: Greg Nori is responsible for launching Sum 41's career and producing their multi-million selling records. "He's responsible for launching some 41's career and all those multimillion selling some 41 records produced by Greg Norrie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Canadian Producers

podcast.title: Caught in African Civil War
podcast.body: During the recording of the "Chuck" album, Sum 41 traveled to the Democratic Republic of Congo with the group War Child to film a documentary on the effects of the Civil War. Ten days into their trip, a ceasefire ended, and they found themselves trapped in a hotel between two warring rebel factions, subjected to mortar rounds, RPGs, and stray bullets. "we were just caught in the middle of it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Chuck Album Recording Location
podcast.body: The "Chuck" album was recorded in a unique, bunker-like studio situated across the street from the Hells Angels headquarters in Toronto. "now we can get to recording the Chuck album, which was recorded in a bunker like studio, across the street, from the hell's angels headquarters in Toronto."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Collaboration with Iggy Pop
podcast.body: In late 2002, Iggy Pop invited Sum 41 to contribute to his "Skull Ring" album, an opportunity Derek Whibley considered a "privilege." Whibley, along with producer Greg Norrie, co-wrote the track "Little Know It All" with Iggy Pop. Whibley felt an immediate connection with Pop during their first phone call and they have maintained contact since, sometimes performing at the same festivals, such as in France in 2016. "Iggy Pop was a great experience, and sort of a privilege."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Crowdsourcing for 13 Voices Album
podcast.body: The album "13 Voices" was uniquely funded by Sum 41 through crowdsourcing, indicating a shift in their financing model. "some 41 funded this record through crowdsourcing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Dave Baksh's Departure & Return
podcast.body: Lead guitarist Dave Baksh quit the band in 2006 due to an argument over musical direction, as he preferred a metal style while Derek Whibley sought a more artistic pop-punk approach. Baksh left to focus on his own group, Brown Brigade, reducing Sum 41 to a trio. He later rejoined the band in 2015 for the "13 Voices" album, and his replacement, Tom Thacker, remained. "Lead guitarist Dave Brown sound quit. I came down to an argument of musical direction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Decline in Popularity (2010s)
podcast.body: This band's popularity in the 2010s was significantly less than it had been previously, reflecting the general decline of the pop punk genre. "Some 41, simple plant and newfound glory were nowhere as big as they had once been."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Derek Whibley's Chronic Back Injury
podcast.body: Derek Whibley first suffered a herniated disc in 2007 on stage in Calgary, an injury he attributes to years of jumping around with a guitar. The condition causes excruciating pain and can temporarily render his legs useless by affecting his spinal cord nerves. Initially, he managed the pain with alcohol and continued touring, preventing proper healing. "I have a herniated disc, which is not a crazy injury, but it does the way... For whatever reason, they're always different for everybody."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Derek Whibley's Chronic Back Pain & Alcohol Use
podcast.body: Derek experienced chronic back pain from extensive touring, which he attempted to manage by drinking alcohol. This continued through a three-year album cycle tour, and worsened significantly during a year-long break from touring in 2013, as he had "no responsibility, no shows, nothing to do and nothing to curb any kind of bad behavior." "My drinking didn't get any better. With a year of that, having no responsibility, no shows, nothing to do and nothing to curb any kind of bad behavior, it just got worse in that year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Derek Whibley's Constant Role
podcast.body: Derek Whibley has been the only constant member of Sum 41 throughout its history, acting as the frontman, guitarist, chief songwriter, and producer, effectively embodying "the band." "He's been the only constant in the group."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Derek Whibley's Self-Production
podcast.body: Derek frequently produced Sum 41's albums, including "Underclass Hero" and "Screaming Bloody Murder," often by necessity when preferred producers like Gil Norton were unavailable, working extensively alone on the music. "Derek didn't want to do it but they couldn't find anybody else so in the end the work fell to him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Derek Whibley's Songwriting Process
podcast.body: Derek's songwriting begins by playing guitar (through a loud, "stun" amp) or piano, focusing on creating a riff that dictates the song's style. He aims for riffs that make him feel "like I want to jump around or move and be like what I'm like on stage." He then creates extensive demos using a drum machine and all possible parts, usually with placeholder "gibberish" melodies, before focusing on actual lyrics, which he often procrastinates on until recording. He collects lyrical fragments but finds full lines emerge with a melody. "Songwriting process for me is kind of how it's always been where I just pick up a guitar or I sit at a piano and I just start playing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Derek Whibley's Writer's Block
podcast.body: Prior to writing "Underclass Hero," Derek Whibley experienced a "paranoid writer's block" and lost confidence in his abilities, leading to him taking nearly a year to write all the songs for the album. "Meanwhile Derek had run into some kind of paranoid writers block. He lost confidence in his abilities which is why it took him nearly a year to write all the songs to the follow up to Chuck."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Early Influence - Gas Station Cassettes
podcast.body: Around 1986, at age six, Derek Whibley discovered "50s and 60s revival hits" on cassette tapes obtained from a gas station promotion, which profoundly contributed to his early love for music. "I just fell in love with those cassettes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Influence - La Bamba Movie
podcast.body: The 1987 movie "La Bamba," which tells the story of Ritchie Valens, significantly influenced Derek Whibley at age seven, making him want to play guitar. "I just fell in love with that movie and I just thought I want to play guitar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Influences - The Monkees and The Beatles
podcast.body: Derek Whibley's interest in music began around age six or seven in 1986, heavily influenced by The Monkees Television Show and The Beatles' music. "I was really obsessed with the Monkeys Television Show, the Beatles music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Mentorship and Demos
podcast.body: Greg Norrie (from Trevor Charger) and Marcos Stanzo (from Len) became friends with Sum 41 after Derek Whibley invited Norrie to their first show. Over a year or two, they helped the band by recording demos, offering advice, and bringing them on tour, playing shows with both Trevor Charger and Len. "Over the next year or two, they both just kind of helped us out. Recorded us, gave us, you know, we did some demos and stuff like that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Extensive Use of Marshall Amplifiers
podcast.body: Sum 41 is listed among hundreds of musicians, both famous and lesser-known, who utilize Jim Marshall's amplifiers. This inclusion underscores the enduring popularity and critical role Marshall amplifiers play in achieving loud, powerful rock sounds across many decades. "Over the decades, Jim's amplifiers became synonymous with loud, powerful rock and today they used by slash, oasis, the death tones, rob zombie, Paul Weller, some 41, pop erosion, hundreds of others, famous and not so famous."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Inventors

podcast.title: First Guitar at 13
podcast.body: Derek Whibley received a fake guitar around age eight, but it wasn't until he was 13 that he got a real guitar, immediately forming his first band in Ajax. "when I got a real guitar I was about 13."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Formation Origin - 41 Days into Summer Vacation
podcast.body: Sum 41 was formed 41 days into the band members' summer vacation in 1996, coinciding with the day the Warp Tour came through their area, which became the inspiration for the band's name. "Because you formed the band 41 days into your summer vacation? 41 into the summer vacation, true."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: Formation and Massive Sales
podcast.body: Sum 41 began in 1996 and went on to achieve significant commercial success, selling a total of 30 million records. "Some 41 started up in 1996 and went on to sell 30 million records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 6: The Punk Revival

podcast.title: Influenced by Blink-182
podcast.body: Sum 41 is recognized as one of the many artists who owe a debt to Blink-182, indicating their influence on the band's musical style or approach within the pop punk genre. "Some 41 good Charlotte simple-plan panic at the disco, followed boy, headly, billy talent, you would meet six, paramour, you know, you get the idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: International Commercial Success
podcast.body: Between 2001 and 2004, Sum 41's albums 'Does This Look Infected' and 'Chuck' all achieved gold or platinum status in multiple major markets including Canada, the US, the UK, and Japan, showcasing their broad international appeal. "all went gold or platinum in Canada, the US, the UK, and Japan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 3: The Return of Rock

podcast.title: Interviewed Band
podcast.body: Sum 41 is among the notable artists and bands that have been interviewed. "Daniel Lannoy, some 41, Billy Corgan..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Meteoric Rise and Burnout
podcast.body: Sum 41 experienced a rapid and intense rise to fame from 1996 to 2005, becoming an international multi-platinum act. However, this period of constant touring and recording, coupled with Derek Whibley's personal health struggles, eventually led to physical and mental exhaustion. "Some 41 went on a meteoric rise from 1996 through to 2005. But you can only burn that hard, that bright for so long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

podcast.title: New Millennium Success
podcast.body: By the new millennium, this band was among the newer acts doing well as skate punk became massive. "Not only were bands like Blink 182, the offspring, MXPX, Pennywise, and No Effects doing well, so were newer bands. Some 41, for example."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Skate Punk

podcast.title: Observation on Contemporary Rock Music
podcast.body: Derek Whibley observes a trend where many rock bands have shifted towards a lighter, more pop, and mainstream sound, seeking commercial success. While he understands this path for others, he notes it doesn't align with Sum 41's approach, and he doesn't perceive a general trend of bands becoming "darker or heavier." "I feel what I find, if I notice anything, I feel like a lot of bands that were rock bands have gone another way, have gone a lot lighter, a lot more pop, trying to be a little bit more mainstream, which is totally fine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Pop Punk Heritage Act
podcast.body: Sum 41 was identified as one of the "Big Heritage Acts" of Pop Punk that kept the spirit of the genre alive in the 2010s, despite its popularity being nowhere near its 90s or 2000s peaks. There was also a sentiment in some punk circles to reclaim punk from "Corporatized Punk" exemplified by bands like Sum 41. "The Big Heritage Acts were still there, you know, offspring, link quantity to some 41 simple plan, and they kept the spirit alive." "There's also the sense in some quarters that Punk needs to be torn down and rebuilt, reclaimed from the so-called Croppered Punk, exemplified by Blink-Wentety 2-Some41 in the offspring."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

podcast.title: Post-COVID Tour Bus Shortage
podcast.body: Following the lifting of COVID-19 restrictions, Sum 41, an internationally successful and multi-platinum band, encountered severe logistical challenges when planning a European tour. Many tour buses had been idle for two years and were not operational, leading to a critical shortage. The few available buses were prohibitively expensive, affordable only to acts like Metallica, forcing Sum 41 to tour Europe in a rented van, reminiscent of their early days. "After the restrictions were lifted, the band wanted a tour Europe. But when they started planning things, they found that there were no tour buses available."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 10: (10-1)

podcast.title: Reasons for Lineup Changes
podcast.body: Derek Whibley attributes the band's lineup changes over the years to members wanting to pursue other interests, the grueling nature of extensive touring, and decisions potentially made during periods of burnout. He states he cannot definitively speak for others' reasons for leaving but offers these observations. "I think the thing with lineup changes over the years comes from probably a few different things."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Steve-O's Support for Famous Stars and Straps
podcast.body: Steve-O of Sum 41 is mentioned as someone who publicly wears gear from Travis Barker's clothing company, Famous Stars and Straps, contributing to the brand's visibility. This highlights collaboration and mutual support among artists in their non-musical endeavors. "and Steve O of some 41".

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Moonlighting

podcast.title: Total Record Sales
podcast.body: Sum 41 has sold "somewhere north of 10 million records" over their career, originating as "suburban brats" who formed a band during summer vacation in the 1990s. "This man has been responsible for tons of hits somewhere north of 10 million records, not bad for a bunch of suburban brats who decided to form a band during summer vacation back in the 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

podcast.title: Unexpected Hit - With Me
podcast.body: The song "With Me," a ballad, became an unexpected hit many years after its initial album release, without being officially promoted as a single or serviced to radio. Its popularity grew organically, entering iTunes Top 10 and being sung by entire festival crowds in Europe, surprising the band. Its success is attributed to the "digital environment," possibly playlists or movie soundtracks, and it garnered YouTube numbers comparable to "Fat Lip." "I was always surprised we had this song called With Me and it was a ballad and we never really thought much of it."

xref.title: Catalog Sale to Harbor View Equity Partners
xref.body: Deryck Whibley sold his song catalog, specifically the songs he wrote for Sum 41, to Harbor View Equity Partners. The exact amount was not disclosed, but he "smiled very, very, very widely" when asked, suggesting a significant payout. "Derek Wibley's song is written for some 41. Another important development of the field of putting song catalogs to work came in 1997, when David Bowie and an investment banker named David Pullman created a financial instrument called Bowie Bonds. To use Wall Street speak, 287 songs from 25 albums recorded before 1990 became asset-backed securities. In exchange for forfeiting royalty income for a period of 10 years, Bowie received an immediate payment of $55 million. He used that money to buy out the rights to songs he lost to his former manager, Tony DeFrees."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

Whibley had an immediate comfortable rapport with Pop during their first 45-minute phone call, feeling like they had known each other already. They have maintained contact over the years, occasionally seeing each other at festivals, such as in France in 2016. "Iggy Pop was a great experience, and sort of a privilege."

xref.body: Cereal Joe was an up-and-coming, young, and talented band that was active around the same time as the early days of Sum 41, both seen as having the potential to achieve significant success. "I remember there was you and another band called Cereal Joe at the time."

xref.body: This group was formed by Dave Baksh after he quit Sum 41 in 2006 to focus on his own musical direction, which leaned more towards metal than the pop-punk evolution Derek Whibley sought. "He left to focus on his own group Brown Brigade."

xref.title: Greig Nori's Management and Production Career
xref.body: Singer Greig Nori became actively involved in managing and producing Sum 41, a band he discovered. He also managed other bands, worked with beer companies, and secured various television gigs. "Singer Greg Norrie has had his hands full with managing and producing a band he discovered. You might have heard of them, they're called Sum41."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the 90s: Part 2

xref.title: Influence on Pop Punk
xref.body: Blink-182 is considered one of the most influential pop punk bands of the 21st century. Their style and career trajectory have left a significant mark on numerous artists across the genre, inspiring bands like Sum 41, Good Charlotte, Simple Plan, Panic! At The Disco, Fall Out Boy, Hedley, Billy Talent, You Me At Six, and Paramore. "Blink has to be considered one of the most influential pop punk bands of the 21st century."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

xref.title: Launching Sum 41's Career
xref.body: Nori is credited with launching the career of Sum 41 and producing their multi-million selling records. "He's responsible for launching some 41's career and all those multimillion selling some 41 records produced by Greg Norrie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Canadian Producers

xref.title: Marriage to Derek Whibley
xref.body: Avril Lavigne was married to Sum 41 frontman Derek Whibley, and their relationship served as inspiration for several songs on Sum 41's "Underclass Hero" album. "including several that he admits being about his relationship with Avril Lavigne, whom he was married."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

xref.title: Predecessor to Sum 41
xref.body: Casper was the band Derek Whibley was in after Chemical Head, and this group ultimately evolved into Sum 41. "after that a band called Casper and then that band turned into some 41."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 1

xref.title: Producer for Pixies and Foo Fighters
xref.body: Gil Norton is a producer known for his work with bands like the Pixies and the Foo Fighters. He was considered to produce Sum 41's "Screaming Bloody Murder" album, but his unavailability led Derek Whibley to produce it himself. "Gil Norton, a guy known for his work with the Pixies and the Who Fighters, couldn't do it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

xref.title: Publishing Catalog Sale (>$30M) (N/A)
xref.body: Deryck Whibley, formerly of Sum 41, sold his entire publishing catalog, including all Sum 41 songs and other works, to Harborview Equity Partners for an undisclosed amount, estimated to be over $30 million USD. Residing in Las Vegas, he benefited from a low capital gains tax rate on this transaction. "Whatever amount he received, although the official number was never made public, it's somewhere north of 30 million US dollars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Songwriting Inspiration for Derek Whibley
xref.body: John Lennon remains a significant songwriting inspiration for Sum 41 frontman Derek Whibley. "John remains a big, big songwriting inspiration for Derek."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

xref.title: Stylistic Contrast for "45"
xref.body: Sum 41's song "45" is explicitly contrasted by Derek Whibley with the style of Rage Against the Machine, clarifying that "45" is not a "rage against a machine song" that calls out specific policies or aims to change opinions, but rather expresses personal frustration. "It's more saying, you're just not my kind of guy. But I'm not really, it's not like a rage against a machine song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Sum 41 Story As Told By Deryck Whibley: Part 2

xref.title: Travis Barker's Clothing Company – Famous Stars and Straps
xref.body: Travis Barker, drummer for blink-182, founded the clothing company Famous Stars and Straps in 1999, based in Corona, California. The brand targets the skate crowd and offers t-shirts, jackets, and hats for men, along with shirts, pants, and bikinis for women, in addition to accessories like belt buckles and bandanas. The company's success is bolstered by famous friends, including Tim Armstrong of Rancid, Steve-O of Sum 41, members of Avenged Sevenfold, and B-Real of Cypress Hill, who wear the brand publicly. Famous Stars and Straps generates millions in annual revenue, and its presence is notable at events like the Warped Tour. "He founded the company in 1999 and targeted the Skate Crowd."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
